E.4 Marine Hydrokinetic Energy Marine energy includes energy generation from wave, tide, and current kinetic movement in oceans, coastal areas, estuaries, and rivers (NLR 2025c). Marine energy resources (wave, tides, currents) are more predictable and less variable than other advanced energy resources, such as wind and solar. This technology offers resilient, point-of-need electricity generation for islands and coastal areas, with the potential to provide 60% of the total domestic U.S. electricity needs (NLR 2025c). By producing electricity locally rather than relying on centralized generation assets located hundreds of miles away, marine energy can increase energy resilience. For example, Oregon’s coastal communities, where there are several U.S. Army National Guard bases, currently depend on electricity generated by inland hydroelectric dams hundreds of miles away. A large-scale wildfire or earthquake could disrupt transmission lines, potentially leaving those coastal regions without power for extended periods. Marine energy could mitigate such risks by enabling coastal self-sufficiency. Although the broad range of different marine energy technologies are still being developed, the deployment of demonstration and full-scale projects, as well as the capacity, in the E.U. exceeds that in the United States. As of 2025, the combined ocean energy capacity in the E.U. totaled 106 GWh, with capacity expected to significantly expand by 2030 (Schuler and Dupont 2025). Although Europe continues to have the most installed wave-energy devices and the greatest capacity, cumulative installations in the rest of the world have, for the first time since 2015, marginally surpassed Europe’s. For example, in July 2022, CalWave Power Technologies Inc. retrieved its xWave wave energy pilot device after a successful 10-month deployment off the coast of San Diego, California. The device, which remained operational for 99% of its deployment, survived two extreme storms, marking a critical milestone in proving wave energy’s commercial viability (DOE WPTO 2023). A U.S. Navy wave energy test site located offshore from a Marine base in Hawaii tests marine energy technologies and connects to a land-based grid using underwater cables (SOEST 2025).
